Last time we found that gas falling into a black hole is the most efficient
way we know of to turn mass into light, and we ended on a question: if you pour
gas in faster and faster, does the black hole just get brighter and brighter?
It does not. The light it makes pushes back on the gas that is trying to fall
in, and at one particular luminosity, set by nothing but the mass of the black
hole, the push wins. **This lecture finds that luminosity, what it means for how
fast a black hole can eat, and what the light from accreting gas looks like.**

## Light pushes

Even though photons have no mass, they have momentum. In
[lecture 3](../special-relativity/index.qmd#e-mc2) we used the fact that a
photon of energy $E$ carries a momentum $p = E/c$. When a photon is absorbed or
scattered by an atom or a particle, momentum is transferred. We are going to
use this fact to derive the Eddington limit, and we will do it in steps.

Consider completely ionized hydrogen uniformly surrounding an accreting black
hole of mass $M$ that is radiating isotropically — equally in all directions —
with a luminosity $L$. We are going to look at the effect on one proton and
electron pair, and we are going to assume that they are "tied" to each other,
which is a decent approximation. If the light pushed the electrons away and left
the protons behind, the separated charges would pull back on each other
enormously hard, so the pair moves as one.

**Gravity pulls on the pair through the proton.** The proton is 1836 times as
massive as the electron, so essentially all of the pair's weight is the
proton's. The gravitational force on it at a distance $r$ from the black hole
is just

$$
F_{\mathrm{grav}} = \frac{G M m_p}{r^2} .
$$ {#eq-fgrav}

**Light pushes on the pair through the electron.** The radiation flux at a
distance $r$ is the one we met in
[lecture 7](../accretion-efficiency/index.qmd#luminosity-and-flux),

$$
F = \frac{L}{4\pi r^2} .
$$ {#eq-flux-again}

The radiation interacts much more directly with the electron, because it has the
smaller mass, which means that we use the **Thomson scattering cross-section**
to describe the interaction between the light and the matter. A cross-section is
an effective target area: how big the electron looks to a passing photon, for
the purpose of scattering it. For an electron it is

$$
\sigma_T = 6.65 \times 10^{-25}\ \mathrm{cm^2} .
$$

The same area for a proton is smaller by a factor of $(m_e/m_p)^2$, about three
parts in ten million, which is why the electron is the one that counts.

The radiation force $F_{\mathrm{rad}}$, measured in dynes
($\mathrm{g\,cm\,s^{-2}}$), is a function of $F$, $\sigma_T$ and $c$, each
raised to the power $+1$ or $-1$ — no squaring, no square roots.

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Use the units of $F$, $\sigma_T$ and $c$ to build a force"}
Write out the units of each ingredient. A flux is an energy per second per
square centimeter, and an erg is $\mathrm{g\,cm^2\,s^{-2}}$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
[F] &= \frac{\mathrm{g\,cm^2\,s^{-2}}}{\mathrm{s\,cm^2}} = \mathrm{g\,s^{-3}} ,
  \\[0.8em]
[\sigma_T] &= \mathrm{cm^2} , \\
[c] &= \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}} .
\end{aligned}
$$

A dyne is $\mathrm{g\,cm\,s^{-2}}$. The grams can only come from $F$, so $F$
appears to the power $+1$, bringing $\mathrm{g\,s^{-3}}$. Multiplying by
$\sigma_T$ adds the $\mathrm{cm^2}$: $\mathrm{g\,cm^2\,s^{-3}}$. That is one
centimeter too many and one second too few — exactly what dividing by
$\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$ fixes. So $c$ appears to the power $-1$:

$$
\left[\frac{\sigma_T F}{c}\right]
  = \frac{\mathrm{cm^2} \times \mathrm{g\,s^{-3}}}{\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}}
  = \mathrm{g\,cm\,s^{-2}} .
$$

No other combination of the three, each to the power $\pm1$, comes out as a
force.
:::

After some playing around, you can see that it is

$$
F_{\mathrm{rad}} = \sigma_T\, \frac{F}{c} .
$$ {#eq-frad}

But let's think about it differently, though still dimensionally. Photons don't
have mass, but they still have momentum, so they are going to transfer some
momentum when they interact with matter. Obviously, the higher the flux, the
more momentum the light will carry — more photons. The larger the area over
which the photons interact with the electron, the larger the effect will be.
Why the $c$? Well, that comes in because the momentum of a photon is
$p = E/c$. Since flux is energy per unit area per unit time, if we divide by
$c$, we get momentum per unit area per unit time, which is actually a
**pressure**: momentum per unit time is force, and force per area is pressure.
This is **radiation pressure**, and $\sigma_T$ is the area it pushes on.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-light-pushes}

1. The Sun's flux at the Earth is
   $F = 1.36 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}}$.

   a. What force does sunlight exert on one free electron at the Earth's
      distance from the Sun?
   b. How does that compare with the Sun's gravitational pull on a proton at
      the same distance?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   **(a)** About $3.0 \times 10^{-29}$ dyn. **(b)** Gravity is
   $9.9 \times 10^{-25}$ dyn, so the light's push is only
   $3.0 \times 10^{-5}$ of the pull.
   :::

2. A $1\,M_\odot$ star becomes a red giant with a luminosity of $100\,L_\odot$
   and a radius of $100\,R_\odot$. Suppose that the outer, very thin layer of
   the star has a mass of $0.1\,M_\odot$ and absorbs all of the radiation
   coming up through it. Remember that force is momentum per unit time.

   a. How much momentum per second does the outer layer absorb?
   b. Compare the force of the light on the outer layer with the gravitational
      force exerted on it by the rest of the star.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   **(a)** $L/c = 1.28 \times 10^{25}\ \mathrm{g\,cm\,s^{-2}}$ — a force of
   $1.28 \times 10^{25}$ dyn. **(b)** Gravity from the remaining
   $0.9\,M_\odot$ is $4.9 \times 10^{32}$ dyn, so the light's push is
   $2.6 \times 10^{-8}$ of it. Absorbing *every* photon still does not come
   close.
   :::

3. Gravity pulls on a proton 1836 times harder than on an electron, while light
   pushes on an electron millions of times harder than on a proton. Explain why
   it is still reasonable to treat the pair as a single particle that feels
   both forces.

:::

## The Eddington limit

::: {.panel-tabset .tracks}

### Physical intuition

The **Eddington limit** is the maximum luminosity a gravitationally bound
object can have before it blows itself — or all the stuff accreting onto it —
apart through radiation pressure.[It is named for Arthur Eddington, who worked
out the same balance for the light pushing outward on the layers of massive
stars.]{.aside .content-visible when-format="html"}

The remarkable thing about it is that **it does not depend on distance**.
Gravity weakens as $1/r^2$, and so does the flux, because light spreads out
over a sphere of area $4\pi r^2$. Both forces therefore fall off at exactly the
same rate, and their ratio is the same everywhere: if the light wins against
gravity at one radius, it wins at every radius, and if it loses at one, it
loses at all of them (@fig-forces).

That makes the limit self-enforcing. If the accretion luminosity were *above*
the Eddington luminosity, it would push the matter away and stop it from
accreting. Then its luminosity would decrease, and it could accrete again. This
is a **feedback**: a black hole that tries to shine brighter than the limit
shuts off its own food supply.

For the Sun, radiation pressure is nowhere near mattering. Its luminosity is
about $3 \times 10^{-5}$ of its Eddington luminosity — the same number as the
ratio of the two forces in the first exercise above, and for the same reason.

### Mathematical explanation

Put @eq-flux-again into @eq-frad:

$$
F_{\mathrm{rad}} = \frac{L\,\sigma_T}{4\pi c\, r^2} .
$$ {#eq-frad-r}

Now we want to see what happens when the radiation force is exactly equal to
the gravitational force of @eq-fgrav:

$$
\frac{L\,\sigma_T}{4\pi c\, r^2} = \frac{G M m_p}{r^2} .
$$

Now solve for $L$ to see what luminosity would just balance gravity:

$$
L_{\mathrm{Edd}} = \frac{4\pi c\, G M m_p}{\sigma_T} .
$$ {#eq-ledd}

Notice that the $r^2$ terms canceled. It doesn't matter how far you are from
the black hole.

*Do the units make sense?* $c\,G M m_p$ has units
$\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}} \times \mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}} \times \mathrm{g}
\times \mathrm{g} = \mathrm{g\,cm^4\,s^{-3}}$, and dividing by $\sigma_T$ in
$\mathrm{cm^2}$ leaves $\mathrm{g\,cm^2\,s^{-3}}$, which is an erg per second.
A luminosity is an energy per second, so yes.

The assumptions behind it are worth saying out loud: spherically symmetric
accretion of fully ionized hydrogen, and completely isotropic radiation. Put in
the numbers and

$$
L_{\mathrm{Edd}} \approx 1.26 \times 10^{38}\,
  \left(\frac{M}{M_\odot}\right)\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}
  \approx 3.3 \times 10^{4}\,\left(\frac{M}{M_\odot}\right) L_\odot .
$$ {#eq-ledd-num}

The Eddington luminosity is simply proportional to the mass, so you can scale
any Eddington luminosity by taking the mass in solar units and multiplying it
by this number.

:::

```{python}
#| label: fig-forces
#| fig-cap: "The forces on one proton–electron pair around a $10\\,M_\\odot$ black hole. Gravity on the proton (solid blue) and the push of the black hole's light on the electron (orange) both fall off as $1/r^2$, so on these logarithmic axes they are parallel lines. At the Eddington luminosity the push equals the pull at every distance; brighter than that, light wins everywhere, and fainter, gravity does."
#| fig-alt: "A log–log graph of force, in dynes, against distance from the black hole, in kilometers, from 100 to one million kilometers. Four straight parallel lines all slope down from upper left to lower right, each falling by a factor of one hundred for every factor of ten in distance. A solid blue line is gravity on the proton. An orange dashed line for radiation at the Eddington luminosity lies exactly on top of the blue line along its whole length. An orange dash-dot line for three times the Eddington luminosity lies above it, and an orange dotted line for three tenths of the Eddington luminosity lies below it, at a constant vertical separation everywhere, so no line ever crosses another."
#| fig-height: 4.03

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.03))

c, G, m_p, sigma_T = 2.99792456e10, 6.6732e-8, 1.6726e-24, 6.6524e-25
M = 10 * 1.9891e33
L_edd = 4 * np.pi * c * G * M * m_p / sigma_T

r_km = np.logspace(2, 6, 200)
r_cm = r_km * 1e5

ax.loglog(r_km, G * M * m_p / r_cm**2, color=BLUE, linewidth=3.0, zorder=2,
          label="gravity on the proton")
for factor, style, label in ((3.0, "-.", r"light at $3\,L_{\mathrm{Edd}}$"),
                             (1.0, "--", r"light at $L_{\mathrm{Edd}}$"),
                             (0.3, ":", r"light at $0.3\,L_{\mathrm{Edd}}$")):
    F_rad = sigma_T * factor * L_edd / (4 * np.pi * r_cm**2) / c
    ax.loglog(r_km, F_rad, color=ORANGE, linestyle=style, zorder=3, label=label)

ax.set_xlabel(r"distance from the black hole  $r$  (km)")
ax.set_ylabel("force on one pair  (dyn)")
ax.set_xlim(1e2, 1e6)
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
plt.show()
```

1. What is the Eddington luminosity of a $1.4\,M_\odot$ neutron star?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   First turn the mass into grams, with a conversion fraction arranged so the
   solar masses cancel:

   $$
   M = 1.4\,M_\odot \times \frac{1.99 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}}{1\,M_\odot}
     = 2.78 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}
   $$

   Substitute into @eq-ledd with the units attached, and no arithmetic yet:

   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   L_{\mathrm{Edd}} = {} & \frac{4\pi
     \left(3.00 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\right)}
     {6.65 \times 10^{-25}\ \mathrm{cm^2}} \\[0.8em]
     & \times \left(6.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\right) \\
     & \times \left(2.78 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}\right)
     \left(1.67 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g}\right)
   \end{aligned}
   $$

   Counting the lower two lines with the numerator, the units on top are
   $\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}} \times \mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}} \times
   \mathrm{g} \times \mathrm{g} = \mathrm{g\,cm^4\,s^{-3}}$. Dividing by
   $\mathrm{cm^2}$ leaves $\mathrm{g\,cm^2\,s^{-3}}$, an erg per second.

   $$
   L_{\mathrm{Edd}} = 1.76 \times 10^{38}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}
   $$

   :::

## The Eddington accretion rate

There is a related rate called the **Eddington accretion limit**, but there is
a little nuance.

Let's consider how much matter per unit time is flowing in toward the black
hole: $\dot M$. In [lecture 7](../accretion-efficiency/index.qmd#the-luminosity-of-accretion)
we wrote the luminosity this produces as

$$
L_{\mathrm{acc}} = \eta\, \dot M c^2 ,
$$ {#eq-lacc-again}

where $\eta$ is the radiative efficiency. We can solve that equation for
$\dot M$,

$$
\dot M = \frac{L_{\mathrm{acc}}}{\eta c^2} ,
$$

and then recognize that $L_{\mathrm{acc}}$ has to be less than the Eddington
luminosity of @eq-ledd, which gives a limit on $\dot M$:

$$
\dot M = \frac{L_{\mathrm{acc}}}{\eta c^2}
  < \frac{4\pi G M m_p}{\eta\, c\, \sigma_T} \equiv \dot M_{\mathrm{Edd}} .
$$ {#eq-mdot-edd}

The nuance is the $\eta$. The limit on *luminosity* is fixed by the mass alone,
but the limit on how fast gas can be fed in also depends on how efficiently
that gas is turned into light. A black hole with a high efficiency reaches the
Eddington luminosity on less gas, so it hits its ceiling sooner. Put in the
numbers, scaled to the standard efficiency of 10%:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot M_{\mathrm{Edd}} &\approx 1.4 \times 10^{18}
  \left(\frac{M}{M_\odot}\right)\left(\frac{0.1}{\eta}\right)\ \mathrm{g\,s^{-1}}
  \\[0.8em]
  &\approx 2.2 \times 10^{-8}
  \left(\frac{M}{M_\odot}\right)\left(\frac{0.1}{\eta}\right)
  M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}} .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mdot-edd-num}

:::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: the fastest a billion-solar-mass black hole can eat"}
**The question.** A $10^9\,M_\odot$ black hole accretes with a radiative
efficiency of 10%. What is the fastest it can accrete, in solar masses per
year, without exceeding the Eddington luminosity?

First the mass in grams, with the conversion written as a fraction so that the
solar masses cancel:

$$
M = 10^{9}\,M_\odot \times \frac{1.99 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}}{1\,M_\odot}
  = 1.99 \times 10^{42}\ \mathrm{g}
$$

Now substitute into @eq-mdot-edd with the units attached:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot M_{\mathrm{Edd}} = {} & \frac{4\pi
  \left(6.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\right)}
  {0.1 \left(3.00 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\right)} \\[0.8em]
  & \times \frac{\left(1.99 \times 10^{42}\ \mathrm{g}\right)
  \left(1.67 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g}\right)}
  {6.65 \times 10^{-25}\ \mathrm{cm^2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Across both lines, the tops carry $\mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}} \times
\mathrm{g} \times \mathrm{g} = \mathrm{g\,cm^3\,s^{-2}}$ and the bottoms carry
$\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}} \times \mathrm{cm^2} = \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}$ (the
efficiency is a pure number). The
cubic centimeters cancel and one power of the seconds cancels, leaving
$\mathrm{g\,s^{-1}}$. *Do the units make sense?* An accretion rate is a mass
per unit time, so yes.

$$
\dot M_{\mathrm{Edd}} = 1.40 \times 10^{27}\ \mathrm{g\,s^{-1}}
$$

Last, into solar masses per year, again with fractions arranged so the grams
and the seconds cancel:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 1.40 \times 10^{27}\ \mathrm{g\,s^{-1}}
  \times \frac{1\,M_\odot}{1.99 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}} \\[0.8em]
& \qquad \times \frac{3.156 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}}{1\ \mathrm{yr}}
  = 22\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}
\end{aligned}
$$

About twenty Suns' worth of gas a year. In lecture 7 we found that one Sun a
year at this efficiency makes a trillion Suns of light, so this black hole, at
its limit, shines at about twenty trillion — which is exactly its Eddington
luminosity from @eq-ledd-num, as it must be.
::::

::: {.panel-tabset .tracks-from-numerical}

### Numerical exploration

Here are @eq-ledd and @eq-mdot-edd side by side, for objects from a neutron star
up to the most massive black holes known.

```{python}
#| label: eddington-ladder

import math

c = 2.99792456e10     # cm s^-1
G = 6.6732e-8         # cm^3 g^-1 s^-2
m_p = 1.6726e-24      # g
sigma_T = 6.6524e-25  # cm^2
M_sun, L_sun, yr = 1.9891e33, 3.83e33, 3.156e7

masses = [1.4, 10, 4.3e6, 1e9, 1e10]
eta = 0.1

head = ["M", "L_Edd", "L_Edd", "Mdot_Edd", "Mdot_Edd"]
unit = ["M_sun", "erg/s", "L_sun", "g/s", "M_sun/yr"]
fmt = "{:>7} {:>9} {:>9} {:>9} {:>9}"
print(fmt.format(*head))
print(fmt.format(*unit))
for m in masses:
    M = m * M_sun
    L_edd = 4 * math.pi * c * G * M * m_p / sigma_T
    mdot = L_edd / (eta * c**2)
    print(f"{m:7.3g} {L_edd:9.2e}",
          f"{L_edd / L_sun:9.2e} {mdot:9.2e}",
          f"{mdot * yr / M_sun:9.2e}")
```

doubles everything, and that raising the efficiency lowers the accretion rate

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-mdot-edd}

1. TON 618 is one of the most massive black holes known, with a mass of about
   $4 \times 10^{10}\,M_\odot$ and a luminosity of
   $4 \times 10^{47}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$.

   a. What fraction of its Eddington luminosity is that?
   b. Assuming a radiative efficiency of 10%, how fast is it accreting, in
      $\mathrm{g\,s^{-1}}$?
   c. Convert your answer to part (b) to $M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   **(a)** About 0.080, or 8%. **(b)** $4.45 \times 10^{27}\ \mathrm{g\,s^{-1}}$.
   **(c)** $71\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$.
   :::

2. Two black holes have the same mass and both accrete at their Eddington
   rates. One is not spinning, with an efficiency of 5.7%; the other spins as
   fast as possible, with an efficiency of 42%. Which is brighter? Which
   swallows gas faster, and by what factor?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   They are equally bright: both shine at the same Eddington luminosity. The
   non-spinning one swallows gas $42/5.7 \approx 7.4$ times faster, because it
   needs that much more gas to make the same light.
   :::

3. A $10\,M_\odot$ black hole in an X-ray binary shines at
   $10^{38}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$. What fraction of its Eddington luminosity is
   that? Could it be accreting ten times faster than it is?

:::

## What accreting matter looks like

What does the spectrum of electromagnetic radiation of an accreting object look
like? We were able to discuss how much energy is released, but not how it looks.
Let's consider two extreme possibilities for accretion onto a **neutron star**.
This is easier than a black hole, because a neutron star has a surface for the
gas to land on, at a radius $R \approx 10\ \mathrm{km}$. Take a typical mass of
$1.4\,M_\odot$. Bright accreting neutron stars shine close to their Eddington
luminosity, which by @eq-ledd-num is

$$
L \approx 1.8 \times 10^{38}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}} .
$$

**First extreme: the whole surface glows.** Suppose all of the energy is
thermalized to some temperature $T_b$ and emitted from the entire surface of the
star, like a blackbody. We use the blackbody luminosity from
[lecture 7](../accretion-efficiency/index.qmd#blackbody-radiation-and-effective-temperature),
$L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$, and solve for $T$ to get

$$
T_b = \left( \frac{L_{\mathrm{acc}}}{4 \pi R^2 \sigma} \right)^{1/4}
  \approx 2 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{K} .
$$ {#eq-tb}

Pretty hot, huh? That's in the X-ray regime.

**Second extreme: every particle hits a shock.** Now let's consider all the
energy going into heating up each electron–proton pair. This happens by slamming
the gas onto the surface of the star and having it stop very quickly. All of a
sudden, the kinetic energy has to go somewhere, and it goes into a **shock**.
We will take the difference between the gravitational potential energy at
infinity (zero) and at the surface, and equate it to a shock energy of
$3kT_s$ — a particle in a hot gas carries an average energy of $\tfrac32 kT$,
and there are two particles in each pair — so that

$$
3 k T_s = \frac{G M m_p}{R} .
$$ {#eq-ts}

For a $1.4\,M_\odot$ neutron star, this is $T_s \approx 7.5 \times 10^{11}\
\mathrm{K}$. This is in the gamma-ray regime.

Astronomers usually quote temperatures like these as the energy $kT$, in
kilo-electron volts ($1\ \mathrm{keV} = 1000\ \mathrm{eV} = 1.60 \times
10^{-9}\ \mathrm{erg}$; the electron volt is from
[lecture 3](../special-relativity/index.qmd#sec-exercises-emc2)). The two
extremes bracket the photon energies:

$$
k T_b \approx 2\ \mathrm{keV} \;\le\; h\nu \;\le\; k T_s \approx 65\ \mathrm{MeV} .
$$ {#eq-photon-range}

Real accreting neutron stars sit somewhere between these extremes, and much of
their light comes out as X-rays.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-accreting-matter}

1. Check @eq-tb. Find $T_b$ for $L = 1.8 \times 10^{38}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$
   and $R = 10\ \mathrm{km}$, and then give $kT_b$ in keV.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   $T_b = 2.2 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{K}$, and $kT_b = 1.9\ \mathrm{keV}$.
   :::

2. A white dwarf has a mass of $1\,M_\odot$ and a radius equal to the Earth's.

   a. What is the shock temperature $T_s$ for gas landing on it?
   b. How many times cooler is that than for the $1.4\,M_\odot$ neutron star?
      Which two properties of the star set the ratio?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   **(a)** $T_s = 8.4 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{K}$, or $kT_s \approx 72\ \mathrm{keV}$.
   **(b)** About 890 times cooler. By @eq-ts, $T_s$ is proportional to $M/R$,
   so the ratio is set by the mass and the radius together — how *compact*
   the star is.
   :::

3. Why does the shock argument need the star to have a surface? What would be
   different for gas falling into a black hole?

:::

## Summary

| Quantity | Expression | What to remember |
|---|---|---|
| Photon momentum | $p = E/c$ | Light carries momentum, so it pushes |
| Radiation force | $F_{\mathrm{rad}} = \sigma_T F/c$ | Acts on the electron; $\sigma_T$ is its target area |
| Gravity | $F_{\mathrm{grav}} = GMm_p/r^2$ | Acts on the proton; the pair moves together |
| Eddington luminosity | $L_{\mathrm{Edd}} = 4\pi c\,GMm_p/\sigma_T$ | About $1.26 \times 10^{38}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ for each solar mass; the same at every distance |
| Feedback | $L_{\mathrm{acc}} < L_{\mathrm{Edd}}$ | Shining brighter pushes away the fuel |
| Eddington accretion rate | $\dot M_{\mathrm{Edd}} = 4\pi GMm_p/\eta c\sigma_T$ | About $2.2 \times 10^{-8}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ for each solar mass, at $\eta = 0.1$ |
| Accreting neutron star | $T_b \approx 2 \times 10^7$ K, $T_s \approx 7.5 \times 10^{11}$ K | Photons from about 2 keV to 65 MeV |

A black hole cannot shine brighter than its Eddington luminosity for long, and
so it cannot swallow gas faster than its Eddington rate. Both limits are
proportional to its mass: the bigger it gets, the faster it is allowed to grow.
Next time we will follow that thought to its end, and ask how long it takes a
small black hole to become a billion-solar-mass monster.
